data.title: Live updates: Relationship with Canada still rocky ahead of UN General Assembly; AI companies hit with new lawsuit
data.description:
The tension between President Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has intensified since the Canadian leader’s visit with the European Union (EU) earlier this week. 

U.S. and Canada have continued to place tit-for-tat tariffs on American and Canadian goods. The relationship has also been stained this week by the European Commission President Ursula Von der Leyen’s proposal to make Canada an associate member of the EU this week, which Trump said would be a “horrible act.”

This comes ahead of Trump’s scheduled appearance at the United Nations General Assembly next week, where international heads of state will gather in New York City as the U.S.’s war with Iran wages past the 200-day mark and Russia’s war with Ukraine escalates.

But there are currently no scheduled meetings between Carney, according to The Hill’s Mallory Wilson and Helen Huiskes.

On Friday, AI companies Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google were all included in a lawsuit alleging “collusion” between the tech giants.

Plaintiffs claim that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk and Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis made an illegal business agreement among competitors by agreeing to slow the development of their AI systems, violating U.S. antitrust law.

The lawsuit points to a recent proposal from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who called for “industry-wide coordination” to “pace the frontier” of Ai development due to recent safeguard concerns.

President Trump is spending the day in Camp David Saturday after arriving late the night before, marking his third trip this year to the presidential retreat in Frederick County, Maryland.

The president is not slated to make any public appearances during his stay at the presidential retreat and will return to the White House on Sunday.

Follow live below.

data.title: Why is the Trump administration targeting  foreign journalists?
data.description:
For more than 40 years, a Reagan-era policy enabled foreign correspondents to stay in the U.S. lawfully as long as their job required. This summer, the Department of Homeland Security announced these journalists will face restrictive new visa requirements that could be abused to punish those critical of the Trump administration.  

The new rules would cap journalists’ initial admission to no more than 240 days (less than eight months), eliminating a flexible and welcoming policy that has lasted decades across both Republican and Democratic administrations.  

Although the U.S. has long been a champion of press freedom, the Trump administration has shown itself to be unabashedly antagonistic toward the media. The new policy disturbingly echoes those found in Russia, China and Iran, which use strict visa compliance rules to punish journalists and media outlets that report on their governments unfavorably. 

Across the government, agencies have taken extreme actions to arrest and charge journalists; issue subpoenas, including to journalists’ family members; shut down access to the White House and the Pentagon; threaten broadcasters; and sue news outlets. The most egregious acts have been tied to the immigration crackdown, including revoking visas, detaining and even deporting foreign journalists.

Taken together, this shows a pattern of hostility unlike any in modern U.S. history, one in which the federal government aims to pacify and impose its views on the free press and imperils the rights enshrined in the First Amendment.

For decades, the Reagan-era policy allowed journalists to work for multiple years, granting them the time and stability needed to build deep networks and trusted contacts, understand and report on American life, build expertise, lease a house, and enroll children in schools. With this flexible system, foreign journalists could broadcast a thorough and nuanced view of America’s story to their home audiences, in their own languages and cultural frames. 

Homeland Security claims, without substantiated evidence, that the new requirements are needed for “national security and fraud prevention.” Yet, by its own admission, the department recognized “the lack of public data cited in the proposed rule regarding fraud and overstays specific” to journalists.

For journalists seeking a longer stay, Homeland Security would compel them to put in an extension application every 240 days to remain in lawful status, incurring additional costs, giving new biometric data, and possibly needing to be interviewed about the content of their reporting. Such intrusive and expansive scrutiny risks granting the government the power to target foreign journalists in connection with their reporting. 

Before arriving in the U.S., foreign journalists undergo thorough security vetting and are interviewed by U.S. diplomats overseas. As such, the U.S. government holds comprehensive information about their resumes, their employers’ information and their purpose of travel. 

The new rule has sent chills among the foreign press community, fearing how the government could go after journalists for their reporting and suppress access to independent information. In this new milieu, foreign journalists are likely to second-guess their editorial decisions and self-censor to avoid running afoul of Homeland Security monitors.

In August, reflecting a profound concern for the right to a free press, the Committee to Protect Journalists and other press freedom advocates called on the U.S. Congress to exercise its power of oversight and to block the rule.

Congress must ensure that the ability of the foreign press to undertake continuous reporting is not obstructed through administrative artifice, recognizing that the Department of Homeland Security also faces a processing backlog and is affected by budgeting disputes and agency shutdowns. 

Thankfully, a federal judge intervened just before the regulations were set to go into effect, after unions and advocacy groups sued the government over the new rules. The judge, F. Dennis Saylor of Boston, said the amended policy was based on “exceptionally weak” rationales. “The weakness of the connection between the rule and its purported rationales,” he continues, “raises legitimate questions as to whether its real purpose is not to safeguard national security and protect our borders, but to achieve other, undisclosed, goals.” 

We should recall that when the Reagan administration adopted flexible and enabling rules for foreign journalists, the United States was championing individual rights and freedoms in its global contest against the now-defunct Soviet Union, which was notorious for repressing free and independent journalism. 

More than 40 years later, the Trump administration has turned its back on America’s proud commitment to liberty for all. Like Saylor, we must continue the fight for open inquiry, transparency and free expression. 

Loghman Fattahi is the U.S. advocacy representative at the Committee to Protect Journalists, an independent, nonprofit organization that promotes press freedom worldwide.

data.title: Lawsuit accuses Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI, Google of AI pacing 'collusion'
data.description:
AI companies Anthropic, OpenAI, Space XAI and Google are being sued over alleged collusion as pressure mounts to slow the rapid development of AI.

The complaint, filed Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, points to a recent proposal from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who called for “industry-wide coordination” to “pace the frontier” as concerns mount over the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI.

“We must slow the space in which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote in a Sept. 12 essay.

The plaintiffs allege that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk and Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis made an illegal business agreement among competitors by agreeing to slow the development of their AI systems, violating federal antitrust law.

Within hours of Amodei publishing his essay, Musk responded, saying “Dario is right,” while Altman also said he agreed with Amodei. Hassabis called the proposal “the right path forward,” according to the complaint.

Nick Rowley, one of the attorneys who filed the lawsuit on behalf of four plaintiffs, said decisions about AI safeguards should be made through government action rather than private agreements among major technology companies.

Rowley said in a statement to Politico that the case was filed to ensure “private self-serving agreements between the world’s most powerful ‘for profit’ technology companies” don’t result in AI “quickly spin[ing] out of human control.”

“Humanity deserves iron clad safeguards when it comes to extinction event threats such as nuclear warfare and now the biggest risk to mankind in history,” Rowley continued. “The rule of law should be established transparently and lawfully by our government, with accountability to the public.”

The plaintiffs include Florida attorneys Charles Buist and Nick Spetsas, Cheyenne Hunt — an attorney who played a key role in exposing the sexual misconduct allegations against former Rep. Eric Swalwell (D-Calif.) — and California resident Christine Bullock.

Amodei’s proposal had already raised antitrust concerns among lawmakers in Washington, after the Anthropic CEO suggested the government could provide a “narrow waiver for certain kinds of safety conversations” so AI companies could work together on standards without violating U.S. antitrust law.

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) rejected the idea during a Senate hearing with FBI Director Kash Patel on Tuesday.

“There is absolutely no world in which I will consent to giving the most powerful companies in the history of the world — a small group of three or four of them — antitrust exemptions so they can what … collude together?” Hawley said. “Absolutely no way that’s happening.”

data.title: Healthy food is the missing piece in health savings and flexible spending accounts
data.description:
Our country is facing a chronic disease epidemic. Sixty percent of American adults have at least one chronic disease and we spend $5.3 trillion a year on healthcare.  

In a political climate where it’s hard to agree on anything, the positive in this case is that there has been a decades-long, widespread alignment that diet and exercise are critical to reversing this trend. As CEO of an organic food provider, I am glad to see things are changing in the right direction. 

So why haven’t we made more progress? As it relates to the food side of the equation, the release of the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s updated dietary guidelines has received a lot of attention, but every version of those guidelines for decades has lifted up the benefit of whole fruits and vegetables and for good reason. 

PLOS Medicine found in a 2019 study that if Americans met their daily fruit and vegetable guidelines, they could prevent 1.93 million cardiovascular events and save $40 billion in U.S. healthcare costs. An apple a day really could keep the emergency room away. Yet only 10 percent of Americans eat the recommended amount of vegetables and only 12 percent eat the recommended amount of fruit. 

This is not a consumer education problem. It’s an access problem. Tightening budgets and rising food costs shift hungry consumers to cheaper and more heavily processed foods.  

On the exercise front, in June, Harvard released a new study that found that long-term resistance training increased your chances of living longer, in fact it represented a 13 percent lower risk of all-cause mortality, 19 percent lower risk of cardiovascular mortality and 27 percent lower risk of neurological disease mortality.  

The percentages are startling, but we’ve known about the link between exercise for so long that our federal government has gone beyond simply encouraging us to go for a run. There’s a reason the IRS allows health savings accounts and flexible spending accounts to pay for exercise apps, gym memberships and equipment.

So why haven’t we made the same possible for healthy food? 

Americans have $160 billion sitting in health savings and flexible spending accounts — pre-tax money specifically earmarked for their health. Under IRS rules, they can spend it on exercise programs, prescription drugs, medical devices, acupuncture and even sunscreen.

But not on an apple. Not on a bag of spinach. Not on the organic blueberries that decades of research show can reduce the risk of heart disease, type two diabetes and certain cancers. On the contrary, a flexible spending account will allow an American family to pay for a type two diabetes drug, Metformin, but it won’t pay for the vegetables that could help someone avoid needing it.

This isn’t just ironic — it’s backwards.  

More than half of American adults — 119 million people — have high blood pressure and have to take blood pressure meds they pay for with their health savings accounts. But those same accounts won’t pay for the foods proven to lower blood pressure without drugs. 

We can fix this. 

We have over $160 billion in health savings account assets and roughly $30 billion in annual flexible spending account contributions, but the IRS definition of health excludes the single most evidence-backed intervention for chronic disease prevention: eating more fruits and vegetables. 

Congress should expand health savings and flexible spending account eligibility to include fresh, frozen and canned fruits and vegetables. Whole produce; not processed food disguised as health food. It takes pre-tax money that workers already earned and already saved for and lets them use it for the foods that prevent disease.  

Congress should amend health savings and flexible spending eligibility to include fruits and vegetables, to allow families to use $500-$1,000 a year of that money to buy healthy fresh food. And on the executive branch side, the Make America Healthy Again Commission should include health savings and flexible spending produce eligibility in its policy recommendations. 

Will this work? Well, we don’t have to look far to make a case. Two programs that empower families, SNAP and WIC, prove consumers will buy healthy food if they have access.  

The Double Up Food Bucks program operates in more than 25 states and provides a $1 for $1 match for SNAP eligible families to buy fresh fruits and vegetables. The WIC program provides participants with a monthly allowance specifically to purchase fresh, frozen and canned fruits and vegetables.  

Guess what happened? The National Institutes of Health found that the Double Up Food Bucks program led people to spend more on fruits and vegetables, buy greater variety, and make them a bigger part of their grocery purchase.

There is even a recent precedent for this. In March 2020, Congress passed the CARES Act, expanding flexible spending account eligibility to include over-the-counter medications. I’d argue fruits and vegetables are the ultimate over-the-counter medicine — good for you, proven to help and something we should make easier for people to afford.

Turning around the chronic disease trends in this country won’t happen overnight. But we can’t afford to leave proven solutions on the table.

It’s time for Congress to act.

Ricky Silver is CEO of organic food provider Daily Harvest.

data.title: Carney's Euro trip inflames Trump tensions
data.description:
The tension between President Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has only intensified amid the latter’s cozying up with the European Union (EU) on a high-profile trip this week. 

The relationship between the U.S. and Canada has been increasingly strained due to tit-for-tat tariffs on American and Canadian goods and Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” along with his repeated remarks about making Canada the 51st state.

Trump lashed out Wednesday against a proposal to make Canada an associate member of the EU, telling reporters it could be considered a “hostile act” and threatening to slap tariffs or stop trading with Europe if it goes ahead. 

The proposal, put forward by European Commission President Ursula Von der Leyen, would be a new status for the bloc and has yet to be clearly defined. Leaders from both sides will meet in Montreal at the end of October, where the proposal to take the Canada-EU relationship to a higher level will likely be discussed in more detail. 

Carney welcomed the proposal in his appearance at the European Parliament on Thursday, although he specified he is not seeking full membership in the EU, but rather more integration in trade and defense to strengthen both Canada and the bloc. 

“We do not seek power to dominate others,” he said. “On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”

The deterioration in relations between the U.S. and Canada is without precedent in what has long been an ironclad alliance. While Carney has touted a geopolitical realignment, he regularly says America remains a crucial partner. 

Still, the rift has already affected both countries, on an economic and social level, as Canadians rethink buying American products and visiting the US as tourists.

Imran Bayoumi, deputy director at the Atlantic Council, said the “volatility coming from the United States” and Canada’s desire to diversify partners explain the latest developments in Europe. 

“I think the Trump driver is the main one, but I think there’s also a recognition that it’s a more dangerous geopolitical world,” Bayoumi said. “Canadian foreign policy is still rooted in a values-based approach and I’m not sure it can be said that the U.S. has that same outlook right now, so I think trying to meet the EU on that same plane is important to Canadians.”

Some senators said Thursday that they’re not surprised Canada is looking elsewhere for allies amid the tension with Trump, but that the U.S.-Canada relationship should be preserved.

“It’s understandable to me that the EU and Canada would look for ways that they can start to build relationships,” Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minn.) said. “You start to want to find new friends.”

Smith said her state is already seeing economic effects of fraying interchange with Canada, which is Minnesota’s largest export market. 

Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.) said the same about his state. 

“We had a lot of Canadians that come across the border to go to restaurants and shop, they don’t do that now,” Peters said. “They’re like, ‘I’m not going to go across to America.’ So, it’s really sad, and for us too to have to deal with that. So hopefully, we’ll get through it. I think it’s a good friendship. It’ll last, but it’s certainly being strained.”

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said the EU membership idea is just both countries entertaining a way to hit back at the U.S. 

“They’re just trying to irritate the United States. They’re just sending a message that they know that Canada is not happy with us,” Rounds said of the EU. “I think it’s unfortunate that that happens, but it’s one more way in which Canada can express their hurt.” 

Rounds, too, said the Canadian relationship was important and that the whole back-and-forth should have a goal. 

“They’re our friends, they’re our allies, and I think the bottom line is, you need to get results at some point,” Rounds said of Canada. “Tariffs have a place, but the end result should be a better relationship when we’re all done.”

Trump told reporters Wednesday that Canada has “been a terrible trade partner” and that he doesn’t see them becoming an associate member of the EU.

“If they do that, if I think it’s at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things,” he said. “So, if they do that, if Europe does that, with a bad intention — if it’s a good intention, that’s fine — if it’s bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe, which is a possibility.” 

Bayoumi said the U.S. “might not love it as a policy,” if Canada and the EU strike a deal.

“But at the same time, if that’s Washington’s position, there are actions that it could also take to start to repair the relationship with Canada,” he said.

Trade negotiations broke down last month between the U.S. and Canada after weeks-long negotiations. Both sides accused the other of adding stipulations last month that were nonstarters. The breakdown led to 50 percent tariffs on billions of dollars of Canadian goods, with Ottawa then announcing dollar-for-dollar counter tariffs on U.S. goods.

The standstill is likely to continue into the fall. While both Trump and Carney are attending the United Nations General Assembly next week, there are no confirmed plans for the two to meet.

Even if things thaw, Carney has said there’s no going back to the previous status quo. 

Carney came into power on a wave of anti-American sentiment and has sought to realign Canada’s relationship to the world as a “middle power” that doesn’t need to rely on “hegemons,” as he described it in January.

“I think the relationship will be different regardless of who’s in power in 2028, regardless of what comes next,” Bayoumi said. “I think you’re going to have a Canada that’s more used to its autonomy, asserting itself, and hyper-focused on its national interest.”

“But I also think the bilateral relationship is going to endure,” he continued. “You can’t change geography, Canada, the U.S. share a land border, share a binational military command, they still have tons of shared interests, close economic ties and so those levels and areas of cooperation are going to persist regardless.”

data.title: Why people in the Northeast will be paying higher heating bills this winter
data.description:
As fuel costs rise amid the U.S.-Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars, Americans in the Northeast may have to pay significantly more to heat their homes this winter. 

With the price of diesel, in particular, increasing, so too will the cost of a home heating fuel known as heating oil or fuel oil that is commonly used in Northeast states.

Nearly 5 million U.S. households used heating oil as their primary heat source in the winter of 2023 through 2024, 82 percent of them located in the northeastern part of the country. 

William O’Neil, principal research analyst at S&P Global, said that heating oil and diesel prices tend to move together, so when diesel prices go up, heating oil usually does, too.

“The price of diesel historically has a pretty strong relationship to the price of heating oil because they’re effectively chemically identical. They just have different additives, different treatments,” O’Neil said. 

He said that those Americans could end up paying nearly 50 percent more this year to heat their homes than they were last year. 

“It would not shock me if Americans or specifically New Englanders are paying something like $2 more per gallon than they were last winter,” O’Neil said. “Residential heating oil prices last winter were something like $3.75 to $4 a gallon, so an additional $2 per gallon on top of that, you’re talking about something in the range of 50 percent higher.”

The National Energy Assistance Directors Association, which represents state-level officials seeking federal funding to help people pay for energy, released its own analysis last week projecting that heating oil could cost 31 percent more this winter than last.

It estimated that the relevant households spent an average of $1,749 on heating oil last winter and projected they could spend $2,297 this winter.

Mark Wolfe, the group’s executive director, said that as diesel costs have risen further, prices may go even higher.

While heating oil saw the most dramatic increase in the group’s analysis, the organization projected that in general, Americans could spend an overall average of 8.7 percent more to heat their homes this winter.

It projected that natural gas could cost 5.8 percent more, electricity could cost 9 percent more and propane could cost 8.7 percent more.

Wolfe noted that higher fuel costs could have significant economic impacts for lower- and middle-income Americans.

“When you have budgets where there’s very little discretionary income, you have to cut back on groceries. You cut back on medicine. Any discretionary activities you don’t do. If you have to, you borrow from payday lenders. Some people fall behind in the utility bills and get shut off from power. It’s a spiraling effect,” he said. 

He noted that this comes on top of high gasoline prices that are also straining Americans’ budgets. As of Friday, the national average gasoline price was about $4.47 per gallon, according to AAA. Diesel, meanwhile, was averaging $6.45 per gallon.

For heating oil specifically, Wolfe said that Americans typically buy the fuel by the beginning of October, meaning the increase could be felt before the midterm elections.

While it’s not entirely clear how this may play out politically, it comes as Maine and New Hampshire face competitive Senate races. 

Wolfe said that he wants Congress to increase funding for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) to offset the high energy cost for the poorest families, saying the situation is “rapidly becoming a crisis in affordability.”

Costs of diesel, gasoline and heating oil are all going up because of both the U.S.-Iran conflict and the Russia-Ukraine war.

More specifically, both the price of crude oil and attacks on refineries that produce the oil are playing major roles.

Tom Kloza, chief oil analyst at Gulf Oil, said that the price of crude was high because of disruptions in the Red Sea.

“The Houthis were always a wildcard, and now the Houthis are very, very active,” Kloza said. 

O’Neil, with S&P Global, also said that for oil, uncertainties about the future of the Strait of Hormuz are a factor, even as there is some movement in the crucial waterway.

“Earlier on in the war, there was there was this working up towards” a ceasefire, he said. “Now we’re in kind of a point where, with the Houthis getting involved, with the strikes on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, which was a vital conduit for oil to be exported out of the Middle East without having to pass through the Strait of Hormuz … It adds it adds a shroud of additional doubt that this war and its oil market implications are going to be resolved really anytime soon.”

On the refining side, Kloza pointed to Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries. 

“The biggest problem for the world right now is that we are about 7 million barrels a day of refining capacity on the sideline and that means that you know refined products prices: gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel, are going to be sky high,” he said.

data.title: NAACP sues to block Trump administration from sending armed agents to polls
data.description:
The NAACP filed a lawsuit Friday alongside other civil rights groups to block the Trump administration from sending armed agents to U.S. polling places ahead of November’s midterm elections.

The lawsuit names the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the Department of Justice (DOJ), the FBI and several Trump officials, seeking to prevent them “from deploying agents in a manner that unlawfully intimidates voters or anyone urging or aiding voters.”

“Defendants’ statements and actions have made voters… afraid of appearing at polling places, helping others vote, serving as election volunteers, and advocating for their political beliefs and preferred candidates,” the NAACP’s lawyers wrote. 

Democratic senators pressed FBI Director Kash Patel earlier this week on whether his agency would comply if President Trump asked him to send agents to the polls. While Patel acknowledged he was aware of laws that prohibited armed officers or troops from polling sites, he also said that he may in the case that there was “a violation of the law.”

“The FBI will follow the law. If there’s a reason to go there because there’s been a violation of law, we will,” Patel said.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin made similar arguments during his confirmation hearing earlier this year, saying, “The only reason why my officers would be there is if there was a specific threat for them to be there, not for intimidation.’

The plaintiffs — also including the National Urban League and the American Federation of Teachers, among other groups — said they fear the presence of armed federal law enforcement officers at polling cites may “expose [voters] to physical violence, surveillance, and harassment if they participate in the electoral process.”

The civil rights organizations also allege the presence of federal agents would violate a section of the Voting Rights Act, which “broadly prohibits intimidation, threats, and coercion—or attempts to do so—throughout every stage of the voting process, including registering to vote, casting a ballot, and counting votes.”

A statement sent to The Hill Friday night, a DOJ spokesperson wrote that the agency “has never said it would send federal law enforcement to polling locations. Any suggestion otherwise is fearmongering.”

They went on to draw connections between threats of federalizing the polls with armed officials to the post-Civil War Reconstruction era, where the government sought to “undermine the civic participation of the formerly enslaved population.”

“Fearmongering about ‘illegal voting’ is the modern version of the racist narratives that were used to justify poll taxes, literacy tests, and arbitrary ‘character’ assessments for generations,” the lawyers continued.

The lawsuit mentioned one case in which officers in Lee County, Florida established an immigration checkpoint on a main access road before a voting precinct that contained a predominantly Black and Latino population.

“Allegations that DHS law enforcement engages in ‘racial profiling’ are disgusting, reckless, and categorically FALSE,” a DHS spokesperson said in a Friday statement to The Hill. “What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is if they are illegally in the U.S.—NOT their skin color, race, or ethnicity.”

The spokesperson continued, “ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations. ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action.”

A similar lawsuit filed by the city of Denver earlier this month similarly sought to block ICE agents from patrolling polling sites, though the case cited a different federal law prohibiting the presence of “troops at polls.”

The DOJ deployed election monitors in recent primaries, including during South Carolina’s GOP runoff GOP and in Rhode Island. DOJ election monitors are typically personnel from its Civil Rights Division.

In August, Trump left the door open to declaring a national security emergency and federalizing control of the midterms, saying “that stranger things have happened” when asked about the possibility.

data.title: Shapiro fires back at RFK Jr., Trump on measles: 'Incompetence'
data.description:
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) fired back against at President Trump’s Friday Oval Office comments calling him a “bad governor” that’s “close to incompetent” following four measles-related deaths in the state.

“Incompetence is letting measles, a disease that was declared eliminated in 2000, reemerge,” Shapiro wrote on social media Friday. “Incompetence is spending your time promoting outright lies instead of urging people to get a vaccination that would protect them against this deadly disease. Incompetence is denying the tragedy of four measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania.”

The president’s diss came immediately after Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the Health and Human Services (HHS) secretary, accused Shapiro of refusing to cooperate with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to address Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak.

“Incompetence is standing right behind you, Mr. President,” he concluded, referring to Kennedy — who stood alongside other Trump administration officials while speaking to press in the Oval Office.

The Keystone State’s measles outbreak has been the focal point of an ongoing bitter political dispute between Shapiro and Kennedy. 

Shapiro criticized Kennedy’s open questioning of whether the deaths in Pennsylvania were directly caused by measles. The secretary, in response, accused the Pennsylvania governor of politicizing the outbreak.

“He doesn’t believe that measles is an issue,” Shapiro said Wednesday. “When I spoke to him over the phone, he wanted to lecture me about natural measles, and in many ways, making excuses.“

Pennsylvania officials on Tuesday reported two additional measles-related deaths, bringing the total for the year to four. This is a record-setting year for measles in the U.S., as the number of cases is at a 35-year high, and there are more related deaths than any year since 1992. 

The deaths have pushed Pennsylvania’s health department to start the process of requesting emergency assistance from the CDC. For the agency to provide assistance, however, it would need to publicly recognize the deaths.

The CDC does not currently report any measles deaths. In a note on its website dashboard tracking the disease outbreak, the CDC says the National Center for Health Statistics “does not currently have any death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause.”

Kennedy has only acknowledged that one of the four people who died with measles-associated conditions passed away as a result of the disease itself. After the Lancaster County confirmed measles as the cause of death for one of the outbreak’s victims, a six-week-old child, the secretary said he “waited for the evidence” before attributing any case to the illness.

Though Kennedy also added that the infant had Amish lethal microcephaly, a rare terminal condition with a typical prognosis of six months from birth.

“They won’t even acknowledge these deaths on their dashboard, something that should have been an administrative process, because it doesn’t fit their phony narrative,” Shapiro added Wednesday. “I think RFK is doing great destruction in this country by stoking this vaccine skepticism.”

The Democratic governor added that the state would not accept federal assistance until the CDC acknowledged the deaths.

Kennedy shot back, saying, “The performance was a replay of the Democrats’ COVID playbook: fearmongering, misinformation, finger-pointing, and the weaponization of infectious disease fears for political gain.”

data.title: Hegseth backs Trump on banning media outlets
data.description:
Welcome to The Hill’s Defense & NatSec newsletter
{beacon}

View Online

Defense &
National Security

Defense &
National Security

 

The Big Story 

Hegseth backs Trump on banning media outlets

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Friday that he “fully supports” President Trump’s decision to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House, claiming those outlets “endangered” U.S. service members with “false stories.” 

AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein

“The Department of War fully supports President Trump’s decision to kick CNN, MSN̶B̶C̶NOW and Politico to the curb so they can publish their Fake News from outside the White House,” Hegseth said in a statement on Friday.  

 

“We are grateful these outlets already chose to self-deport from the Pentagon,” the defense secretary added. “They endangered our troops with false stories, leaks, and trafficked in fiction and lies about the President, our Warriors and their mission.” 

 

Trump said the ban is set to be in effect immediately, happening “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”

 

“It’s really just cumulative stories over the last two years. You get sick of it,” the president told reporters at the White House, adding that more news outlets could be banned in the future. 

 

Hegseth’s endorsement of Trump’s decision comes as the defense secretary has imposed his own media restrictions since taking the helm at the Pentagon.

 

His policies have barred journalists from large portions of the department from walking freely without an escort and have prevented reporters from retaining their Pentagon credentials unless they agree to publish only unclassified information approved by current U.S. defense officials. 

 

Hegseth and his allies have argued those measures are necessary to safeguard critical national security information and prevent unauthorized leaks. 

 

Those opposed to the policies, including news outlets and press freedom advocates, have argued that the Pentagon is stymying independent reporting. 

 

Trump’s Friday ban was panned by both CNN and Politico, stating they will defend their First Amendment rights. 

 

The ban was also criticized by some Fox News contributors, arguing it sets a bad precedent and could backfire in the long-term.

data.title: Hawley invites Flock, Axon, other surveillance tech CEOs to testify
data.description:
Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) invited the CEOs of Flock Safety and other prominent AI-powered surveillance camera manufacturers to testify before the upper chamber’s Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism next week.

Hawley, the subcommittee’s chair, wrote on social media Friday that he “invited the CEOs of Flock Safety, Axon, Motorola and Verkada to testify in front of my committee NEXT WEEK.” Each of the companies the senator listed produce AI-based automatic license plate recognition (ALPR) cameras — which have been scrutinized on both sides of the aisle.

“Americans deserve answers,” Hawley added. 

The Republican’s letters invited Flock’s Garrett Langley, Axon’s Rick Smith, Motorola Solutions’ Greg Brown and Verkada’s Filip Kaliszan to testify on Sept. 23 as part of his investigation into privacy concerns surrounding these ALPRs — which several jurisdictions have removed following reports of data misuse.

The Hill has reached out to the four companies for comment; Flock Axon and Motorola Solutions did not immediately respond to the request.

A Verkada spokesperson told the Hill that Kaliszan is “unable to attend next week’s hearing.”

“We are in communication with the Subcommittee and are providing information to assist Chairman Hawley and Ranking Member Durbin as they prepare for the hearing,” the spokesperson said. “As we’ve explained to the Subcommittee, none of our customers can search a national Verkada network – because none exists. Our customers can only access the data in their own systems.”

The senator has cited concerns with these companies’ citizen data collection and retention policies, as Flock cameras — for example — share information across a national network.

In a previous letter to Langley, announcing his investigation into Flock, Hawley cited St. Charles County Police Department — who terminated its contract with the surveillance camera company after an audit revealing an officer used its database for personal reasons. 

Over 170 contracts have been cancelled with Flock alone, according to anti-surveillance group DeFlock.

Hawley’s first letter also referenced a case in Milwaukee, where prosecutors charged a police officer for allegedly using Flock’s database to search his girlfriend’s license plate 124 times and her former boyfriend’s plate 55 times. The officer entered “investigation” as his reasoning behind each search, but the system never flagged these searches.

On Sept. 3, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) unveiled the Flock-Off Act in the House, which would block the use of federal funding for ALPRs and biometric surveillance cameras. 

Massie said in a press release that cities and police departments have used the technology to turn “their communities into a version of ‘1984,’” George Orwell’s famous dystopian novel.

The issue has divided key figures within the GOP, with President Trump voicing his support for the technology Sunday.

“No, I sort of like [Flock cameras] because of that, because of law enforcement. But some people don’t. They think it’s an infringement,” the president said, adding, “I like them.”
